release.title: Jerry's AI Field Manual
release.headline: Your bottleneck is not finding stronger AI. It is building enough judgment to specify, inspect, and own what the AI ships.
release.summary: Jerry is unusually strong at pushing an agent toward a useful outcome and rejecting shallow answers. The recurring weakness is that acceptance criteria, system understanding, and reusable checks often arrive after the build. This guide turns that pattern into five substantial practice reps and a small role-based X portfolio.
limits: This is a bounded graph audit, not a claim to have read all of X.
The public app stores representative examples and judgments, not timelines, private transcripts, or Jerry's browsing history.
Current-feed judgments become stale. Re-audit a person before treating a six-week-old feed decision as current.
No X follow, list, like, repost, bookmark, message, or account action was taken.

strengths.title: You reject shallow relevance
strengths.detail: You repeatedly pushed past keyword matches, follower prestige, and unexplained demos until the causal reason and your use case were explicit.

strengths.title: You drive to a real artifact
strengths.detail: Your strongest Codex sessions end in a deployed page, verified workflow, or concrete recommendation rather than a generic answer.

strengths.title: You think across product and human context
strengths.detail: You naturally ask why a mechanism matters, who can operate it, what role you should play, and whether the result changes a real decision.

gaps.title: Define proof before autonomy
gaps.verdict: You often discover the real definition of done by rejecting late outputs.
gaps.observed: Recent site, research, and curation threads needed repeated corrections such as ‘not one layer,’ ‘explain why this matters to Jerry,’ and ‘push all the way to production.’ Those are good judgments, but they arrived after work had already expanded.
gaps.cause: The request names the desired outcome but not always the evidence that would falsify a polished result.
gaps.counterevidence: Once the missing bar is visible, you are decisive and willing to demand a complete rerun.
gaps.transferTest: Before the next large task, another person should be able to read your acceptance matrix and predict whether the result passes without asking you for taste corrections.

gaps.title: Make understanding keep pace with output
gaps.verdict: Codex can finish systems faster than you can explain or debug them.
gaps.observed: You correctly noticed that an advanced post such as autoresearch is useless unless you commit to applying it. The same boundary appears in software work: a working interface can look finished while its state, cache, permissions, and failure path remain outside your mental model.
gaps.cause: The agent is optimized to remove mechanics; that also removes the friction that normally builds a system map in your head.
gaps.counterevidence: When given a first-principles pipeline, you ask strong product, ownership, and boundary questions rather than pretending to be the senior engineer.
gaps.transferTest: Explain one shipped feature's input → state → side effect → failure path without Codex, then repair an injected failure using that map.

gaps.title: Compile repeated corrections into guardrails
gaps.verdict: Your taste lives in conversations more than in tests, schemas, and reusable instructions.
gaps.observed: The same classes recur across tasks: shallow source selection, reputation transfer, hidden prerequisites, incomplete production proof, and UI that exposes implementation instead of the decision.
gaps.cause: A correction fixes the current artifact, but the next task begins without a machine-checkable version of that lesson.
gaps.counterevidence: You already notice repeated failure classes. The missing move is encoding one after its second occurrence.
gaps.transferTest: A validator or checklist must fail on a plausible old-style bad output and pass on the corrected one.

gaps.title: Separate interesting from activatable
gaps.verdict: You can collect advanced ideas before the prerequisite project, metric, or skill exists.
gaps.observed: Autoresearch, model launches, demos, and benchmark claims became useful only after you forced the explanation to name what you could retain without building and what commitment actual use required.
gaps.cause: Tech Twitter compresses months of background into a confident post and makes recognition feel like understanding.
gaps.counterevidence: You explicitly rejected context-free Karpathy and Ghostty references once the gap became visible.
gaps.transferTest: Every saved technical post gets one of three outcomes: a no-build rule, a scheduled project with prerequisites, or a deliberate discard.

gaps.title: Treat new agents as untrusted operators first
gaps.verdict: Capability excitement can outrun permission and data-flow inspection.
gaps.observed: The Grok Build discussion mattered only when reframed from launch popularity to a concrete trust failure: what a coding agent transmitted was broader than what a user might infer from visible reads.
gaps.cause: Product UI and marketing describe intended controls; they do not fully reveal runtime egress, storage, or blast radius.
gaps.counterevidence: You quickly converted the incident into the right practical lesson: be careful with newer tools, especially on real repositories.
gaps.transferTest: A new agent touches only a synthetic canary repo until you can state its permissions, outbound data, storage policy, and rollback path.

gaps.title: Bound parallel agents with ownership and stop rules
gaps.verdict: Persistence and parallelism can become coordination debt when each worker lacks one artifact and one closing proof.
gaps.observed: A prior push for maximum parallel work created duplicate watchdog behavior and uncertainty about which thread or artifact actually owned completion.
gaps.cause: ‘Keep going,’ ‘use more agents,’ and ‘show progress’ are different requirements but were treated as one control strategy.
gaps.counterevidence: Jerry wants substantial long-running work, not superficial speed; a small queue with explicit ownership preserves that ambition.
gaps.transferTest: A large task uses one coordinator, at most two or three bounded workers, one deliverable per worker, and no duplicate watchdog threads.

studyPlan.title: Write the acceptance matrix before Codex starts
studyPlan.why: This reduces the expensive late loop where you recognize the real bar only after a polished build exists.
studyPlan.output: One task brief with Must pass, Nice to have, Non-goals, Allowed actions, and Evidence required.
steps: Choose one real personal build or research task—not a toy exercise—and cap parallel workers with one named artifact each.
Write five to eight observable pass conditions and two plausible ways a polished answer could still be wrong.
Name external-write authority explicitly: what Codex may read, change, deploy, or send.
Ask Codex to map every requirement to proof before implementation, then use the same matrix in the final audit.
studyPlan.doneWhen: The final handoff has a requirement → proof table, and at least one check would have caught an earlier shallow result.
studyPlan.codexPrompt: Before building, turn this request into an acceptance matrix. Separate Must pass, Nice to have, Non-goals, allowed external actions, and exact evidence. List two polished-looking failure modes. Do not implement until the matrix covers the real outcome. At the end, prove each row against current state.

studyPlan.title: Own one generated feature end to end
studyPlan.why: A working interface is not ownership if you cannot predict where its data lives or repair a failure.
studyPlan.output: A one-page system map plus one failure you injected and repaired.
steps: Pick one shipped feature with state, caching, or a network boundary. This PWA is a good candidate: source → data → worker/cache → GitHub main → Render → iPhone.
Draw input → transformation → stored state → visible output → failure fallback.
Explain every box aloud without asking Codex to write the explanation.
Inject one safe failure, diagnose it with logs/devtools/tests, and repair it in a coherent small diff.
studyPlan.doneWhen: You can answer where state lives, what happens offline, what can corrupt it, and which test proves recovery.
studyPlan.codexPrompt: Teach me this feature as an owner, not a spectator. First ask me to explain its input, state, side effects, and failure path. Correct my map. Then propose one safe injected failure. Do not repair it for me immediately; guide my inspection until I can identify the boundary, then review my fix and require a regression test.

studyPlan.title: Turn one repeated rejection into automation
studyPlan.why: A correction becomes leverage only when the next task cannot silently repeat it.
studyPlan.output: One validator, regression test, or reusable review rule with a failing fixture.
steps: Choose a rejection that occurred at least twice: shallow source, borrowed reputation, missing prerequisite, or unproved production state.
Write the smallest bad fixture that reproduces the failure.
Add a deterministic check before an LLM judge wherever possible.
Run the check against both the bad fixture and the corrected artifact.
studyPlan.doneWhen: The old failure demonstrably fails without relying on your memory or taste in the moment.
studyPlan.codexPrompt: Find one correction I have made at least twice in this project history. Propose the narrowest deterministic guardrail. Create a plausible failing fixture first, prove it fails, implement the guardrail, then prove the corrected artifact passes. Keep the rule scoped so it does not encode unrelated taste.

studyPlan.title: Build a tiny personal agent benchmark
studyPlan.why: Model reputation and viral demos do not predict performance on your actual task and harness.
studyPlan.output: Three recurring tasks scored on pass/fail, wall time, intervention count, and total cost when available.
steps: Choose three tasks you can judge reliably: one code change, one source-backed research task, and one structured writing or data task.
Freeze the inputs, acceptance checks, and allowed tools.
Run the same task through two products or configurations without changing the rubric afterward.
Keep failures and interventions, not just the best screenshot.
studyPlan.doneWhen: A tool choice changes because of your repeated results—not a launch post or someone else's leaderboard.
studyPlan.codexPrompt: Help me design a three-task personal agent benchmark. The tasks must be repeatable and independently judgeable. Freeze inputs, permissions, and acceptance checks before runs. Record pass/fail, wall time, intervention count, and cost. Do not declare a winner from one run or silently change the rubric.

studyPlan.title: Run the new-tool canary before a real repo
studyPlan.why: The visible files an agent opens are not necessarily the full data it transmits or stores.
studyPlan.output: A synthetic repository test with known canaries, permission notes, observed requests, and a go/no-go decision.
steps: Create a fake repository with harmless unique strings in tracked, ignored, history-only, and environment-style files.
Grant the narrowest read-only or sandboxed permissions available.
Inspect documented data use and, when stakes justify it, observable network requests or local logs.
Record what was accessed or transmitted, what remains unknown, and whether a real repository is allowed.
studyPlan.doneWhen: You can state the tool's blast radius and uncertainty without claiming that upload equals training or theft.
studyPlan.codexPrompt: Design a harmless canary-repo trust test for this new coding agent. Include tracked, ignored, history-only, and environment-style canaries; use no real secrets or work data. Separate what the UI shows, what documentation promises, what runtime evidence observes, and what remains unknown. End with a bounded go/no-go recommendation.

foundationsShelf.title: Julia Evans · software fundamentals
foundationsShelf.why: The best beginner bridge in this curriculum for Git, HTTP, DNS, terminals, CSS, logs, and debugging. Use the site when a real failure exposes a missing noun; no X follow is required.

foundationsShelf.title: MDN · Progressive web apps
foundationsShelf.why: Use while tracing this app's manifest, service worker, offline cache, install scope, and browser lifecycle.

foundationsShelf.title: Simon Willison · agentic engineering patterns
foundationsShelf.why: Concrete tests, source control, verification, and tool patterns for a project you already own.

foundationsShelf.title: Hamel Husain · evaluation guide
foundationsShelf.why: A practical bridge from vague quality complaints to trace review, failure categories, and human-validated checks.

cultureClusters.name: Builders and maintainers
cultureClusters.examples: Simon Willison, Mitchell Hashimoto, Armin Ronacher
cultureClusters.postType: Source releases, implementation notes, benchmarks, bugs, and postmortems.
cultureClusters.gain: Mechanisms you can inspect and operating rules you can reuse.
cultureClusters.risk: Their favorite developer tools may be irrelevant to Jerry, and personal workflows remain anecdotes.
cultureClusters.readRule: Follow the artifact; ask what was measured, what failed, and whether the product itself matters to you.

cultureClusters.name: Reliability and evaluation practitioners
cultureClusters.examples: Cindy Sridharan, Hamel Husain, Shreya Shankar
cultureClusters.postType: Failure taxonomies, traces, observability, debugging, and evaluation methods.
cultureClusters.gain: They turn ‘the AI feels good’ into failure classes, checks, and ownership boundaries.
cultureClusters.risk: Consulting, courses, and specialist infrastructure can make a simple problem look like a program.
cultureClusters.readRule: Keep the smallest method that changes your next task; skip the full stack until real failures justify it.

cultureClusters.name: Lab and product insiders
cultureClusters.examples: Boris Cherny, Thariq Shihipar, Peter Steinberger
cultureClusters.postType: Product behavior, launch context, internal workflows, quotas, and feature framing.
cultureClusters.gain: Fast mechanism truth and vocabulary from people close to the product.
cultureClusters.risk: Employer, launch, and adoption incentives; insiders are not neutral model comparators.
cultureClusters.readRule: Trust direct product behavior in their lane, then seek independent comparison for quality or safety.

cultureClusters.name: Researchers and fundamentals teachers
cultureClusters.examples: Andrej Karpathy, François Chollet, Sebastian Raschka
cultureClusters.postType: Mental models, papers, benchmarks, code notebooks, and research hypotheses.
cultureClusters.gain: Durable concepts that survive a product launch cycle.
cultureClusters.risk: High prerequisite cost; recognition can masquerade as understanding.
cultureClusters.readRule: Either extract one no-build principle or commit the metric, code, compute, and review time.

cultureClusters.name: Interface and explanation designers
cultureClusters.examples: Amelia Wattenberger, Chip Huyen, Eugene Yan
cultureClusters.postType: Visual explanations, long-form guides, workflow diagrams, and prototypes.
cultureClusters.gain: Better ways to see a system and preserve human judgment.
cultureClusters.risk: Low posting cadence and beautiful prototypes that are not production evidence.
cultureClusters.readRule: Use their owned essays and artifacts as a study shelf rather than demanding a daily feed.

cultureClusters.name: Curators, conference hosts, and scene connectors
cultureClusters.postType: Who is emerging, conference clips, vocabulary, forecasts, and compressed takes.
cultureClusters.risk: Commercial media incentives and repeated claims that look like corroboration but share one source.
cultureClusters.readRule: Use them to find an edge, then leave for the original person, code, paper, or conversation.

cultureClusters.name: High-volume meme and reaction radar
cultureClusters.postType: Outages, limits, product drama, jokes, demos, and fast reactions.
cultureClusters.gain: What Tech Twitter is talking about before careful writers publish.
cultureClusters.risk: Velocity, confidence, and engagement are not evidence; the feed can consume all attention.
cultureClusters.readRule: Sample as radar. Never act on a single reaction without a primary source or reproducible test.

cultureClusters.name: Demo, aggregator, and launch accounts
cultureClusters.examples: One-take product clips and benchmark brand accounts
cultureClusters.postType: Polished wins, leaderboards, copied clips, and context-free before/after posts.
cultureClusters.gain: A quick hypothesis or product to test.
cultureClusters.risk: Cherry-picked runs, missing failures, borrowed authority, and no transferable method.
cultureClusters.readRule: Usually cut. Admit only when the underlying artifact and evaluation can be inspected.

people.name: Simon Willison
people.lane: Independent tool inspection, security, and agentic engineering
people.whyLegit: Django co-creator and Datasette creator; his owned writing repeatedly includes code, sources, corrections, and runnable artifacts.
people.whyJerry: He demonstrates the exact loop Jerry needs: inspect a new system, explain the mechanism, build a tiny artifact, and state the boundary.
people.doNotInfer: High volume and strong inspection do not make every tool safe or every sponsored preview neutral.
people.incentive: Consulting, sponsors, vendor previews, credits, and high-volume publishing; prefer source-backed posts.
people.feed: Six-plus current posts sampled; repeated original code and inspection, mixed with small demos and personal experiments.
people.readRule: Home feed, but open only posts with a mechanism, artifact, or failure boundary.

feedAudit.note: High volume; count only artifacts, mechanisms, investigations, and corrections.

representative.label: Inspected the newly open-sourced Grok Build codebase
representative.paraphrase: Instead of repeating the launch, Simon inspected the 844k-line Rust repository, documented what it does, then extracted its Mermaid renderer into a WASM demo.

trustEvents.reason: Repeated source-backed tool analysis across the current feed.
Fresh Grok Build inspect → explain → build sequence strengthened the recurring-method case.

people.name: Mitchell Hashimoto
people.lane: Systems craft, bounded automation, and careful performance claims
people.whyLegit: HashiCorp cofounder, Terraform co-creator, and part of the initial engineering teams behind Vagrant, Packer, Consul, Terraform, Vault, and Nomad; still ships inspectable open-source systems.
people.whyJerry: His useful pattern is not ‘use Ghostty.’ It is narrow permissions, explicit measurements, honest null results, and human verification before action.
people.doNotInfer: Terraform credibility does not make every AI opinion correct, and one personal invoice result is not a general success rate.
people.incentive: Builds and promotes Ghostty, a terminal app. That proves ongoing craft; it does not make Ghostty relevant to Jerry.
people.feed: Five fresh posts sampled: invoice audit, Sol Ultra comparison, Ghostty memory test, Bun rewrite methodology, and one personal post; four contained concrete method or limits.
people.readRule: Home feed for builder judgment; skip terminal details unless the method transfers.

feedAudit.note: Invoice audit, Sol comparison, Ghostty measurement, and rewrite methodology all exposed controls or limits.

representative.label: Read-only construction-invoice audit
representative.paraphrase: He gave an agent read-only email access, restricted sending to himself, received a report, and manually verified findings before contacting anyone.

trustEvents.reason: One excellent workflow, but the initial feed sample looked Ghostty-heavy.
A broader fresh sample showed four method-rich posts and explicit null/limit reporting; promoted for builder judgment, not fame.

people.name: Cindy Sridharan
people.lane: Reliability, observability, debugging, and code ownership
people.whyLegit: Author of O'Reilly's Distributed Systems Observability and a long record of primary reliability writing grounded in real systems.
people.whyJerry: Her current argument targets Jerry's largest risk directly: if an agent wrote a system you cannot understand, debug, or divide into coherent changes, you do not own it.
people.doNotInfer: Reliability authority is not frontier-model or product-ranking authority.
people.incentive: Low promotional pressure in the sampled feed; specialist infrastructure content can still be too advanced for Jerry.
people.feed: Four fresh posts directly covered code ownership, asking basic questions, historical context, craft, and coherent diffs; low engagement but high lane fit.
people.readRule: Home feed despite low popularity; translate each post into one ownership check.

feedAudit.note: Low cadence; all four current posts reinforced ownership, context, debugging, or coherent-diff judgment.

representative.label: Generated code still needs an owner
representative.paraphrase: If Claude produced code you do not understand, you cannot reliably debug, operate, or take responsibility for it.

trustEvents.reason: Strong reliability boundary but only three current posts had been sampled.
Four fresh, coherent ownership posts mapped unusually closely to Jerry's recurring production gap.

people.name: Hamel Husain
people.lane: Production AI evaluation and failure analysis
people.whyLegit: Long ML engineering record at Airbnb and GitHub, dozens of applied AI projects, and owned guides that expose traces, labels, judge validation, and limitations.
people.whyJerry: He turns vague dissatisfaction into a concrete product question: if outputs are hard to evaluate, the task or interface may be underspecified.
people.doNotInfer: Not every task needs a large evaluation program, and his course does not make his tools the only path.
people.incentive: Sells consulting, a live course, and a forthcoming book; prefer posts with real traces, methods, or sample sizes.
people.feed: Seven current posts sampled; repeated original eval methods plus course/community promotion.
people.readRule: Home feed; take the smallest eval method and ignore the program until a real failure corpus exists.

feedAudit.note: Methods and current tool criticism recur alongside course/community promotion.

proofs.label: O'Reilly author record for a forthcoming book

representative.label: ‘Hard to eval’ can be a product smell
representative.paraphrase: When nobody can state what a good output looks like, the product surface may be wrong; adding a grader cannot repair an undefined job.

trustEvents.reason: Repeated method-backed evaluation guidance in a seven-post sample.
Current Fable quota critique remained concrete and commercially adverse rather than launch cheerleading.

people.name: Shreya Shankar
people.lane: Human-centered evaluation, data systems, and adaptive failure taxonomies
people.whyLegit: Berkeley EECS PhD, incoming CMU professor, and owner of inspectable systems including DocETL and EvalGen with primary research behind them.
people.whyJerry: Her work explains how to name new failure classes and make each long Codex task improve the next one.
people.doNotInfer: A taxonomy is inert unless Jerry labels actual failures and reruns the checks.
people.incentive: Promotes tools, research, a course, and a book she helped create; methods and artifacts remain inspectable.
people.feed: Low-to-medium cadence but repeated current posts link owned artifacts and concrete evaluation methods.
people.readRule: Home feed; save only posts that change a failure category or test.

feedAudit.note: Low-to-medium cadence with repeated owned artifacts and evaluation methods.

representative.label: Use an artifact to find concrete document failures
representative.paraphrase: Her current DocETL example converts a vague ‘our docs are bad’ complaint into inspectable error categories.

trustEvents.reason: Six-post sample showed recurring artifact-backed evaluation guidance.
Fresh owned-tool example preserved the same inspect → categorize → improve method.

people.name: Andrej Karpathy
people.lane: First-principles AI education and experimental research workflows
people.whyLegit: Built and taught foundational deep-learning systems and publishes inspectable code, lectures, and experiments such as autoresearch.
people.whyJerry: His best value is a durable principle—objective feedback enables useful autonomy—not a demand that Jerry reproduce advanced research loops.
people.doNotInfer: A Karpathy repost does not transfer his authority to the reposted person, and an advanced artifact is not automatically actionable.
people.incentive: High status causes the network to over-amplify his links; the current feed is sparse and repost-heavy.
people.feed: Current profile sample was mostly selective reposts and short reactions; use projects and long-form artifacts, not daily-feed completeness.
people.readRule: Study shelf. Open only with a translation question or a real prerequisite-matched project.

representative.label: Autoresearch experiment loop
representative.paraphrase: A code agent repeatedly changes a training experiment against a fixed evaluator. The idea is powerful; running it is a project with code, metric, compute, sandbox, and review—not a tip.

trustEvents.reason: Activation audit correctly moved autoresearch to project-only.
Sparse repost-heavy current feed reinforced artifact-first use and the no-reputation-transfer rule.

people.name: Boris Cherny
people.lane: Claude Code workflows and product-insider engineering practice
people.whyLegit: Creator/lead voice around Claude Code with direct product and engineering experience; his strongest posts expose concrete team practices.
people.whyJerry: His automation rule maps directly to repeated Jerry corrections: the second recurring review rejection should become a test, instruction, or CI check.
people.doNotInfer: Claude Code affiliation makes him a strong mechanism source, not a neutral cross-product evaluator.
people.incentive: Anthropic/Claude Code product adoption; much of the current feed amplifies launches and colleague posts.

people.readRule: Study/search, not scarce home attention. Keep originals with methods; skip amplification.

representative.label: Repeated review feedback is an automation failure
representative.paraphrase: Tests, lint, CI, comments, skills, and project instructions should encode repeated team knowledge; a counterpoint warns that speed without craft can automate meaningless output.

people.name: Armin Ronacher

people.readRule: Study shelf for a deliberate fundamentals track; otherwise skip without guilt.

deepDives.title: Grok Build: important as a trust test, not because it is popular

source.paraphrase: Simon inspected the newly open-sourced Grok Build codebase and built a small extracted artifact instead of repeating launch claims.

layers.label: 1 · Exact claim
layers.text: Grok Build is SpaceXAI/xAI's terminal coding-agent harness: a Rust application that can search, edit, run commands, and manage long tasks. The source release made the client inspectable.

layers.label: 2 · Recent-feed pattern
layers.text: Simon repeatedly follows inspect → explain → build. In the same day he documented the large Rust repository and extracted its Mermaid renderer into a WebAssembly demo. That recurrence, not the launch's popularity, earns attention.

layers.label: 3 · Owned artifact
layers.text: The official Apache-2.0 repository is public and states that it is synced from a monorepo and does not currently accept external contributions. Open source lets people inspect this client version; it does not reveal every server behavior.

layers.label: 4 · Counterevidence and incentive
layers.text: An independent canary-repo wire analysis reported that a tested version uploaded a git bundle containing unread files/history and .env canary contents even with model improvement off. That shows transmission/storage broader than a user might infer. It does not establish training or code theft. xAI's stated controls and the independent runtime observation must remain separate claims.

layers.label: 5 · Jerry activation
layers.text: Do not install Grok Build because Tech Twitter discussed it. Keep one operating rule: test a new agent in a synthetic canary repo, start read-only/sandboxed, inspect permissions and data policy, and use runtime evidence when the repository is sensitive.

deepDives.title: Mitchell matters; Ghostty mostly does not

source.paraphrase: A permission-bounded invoice audit produced a report that Mitchell manually verified before taking action.

layers.label: 1 · Exact claim
layers.text: A read-only agent searched years of email and invoice context, could only send to Mitchell, surfaced roughly $45K of confirmed errors, and left every consequential action to a human.

layers.label: 2 · Recent-feed pattern
layers.text: The surrounding sample also included a two-day Sol Ultra comparison with no tangible quality gain, a Ghostty memory reduction with an explicit ‘no measured I/O effect’ limit, and a clean-context Bun rewrite methodology. The pattern is measured builder judgment, not AI hype.

layers.label: 3 · Owned artifact
layers.text: Mitchell co-founded HashiCorp, co-created Terraform, and worked on the initial engineering teams behind Terraform, Vault, Vagrant, and other foundational tools. Ghostty is his newer terminal emulator. Jerry does not need a new terminal to benefit from his reasoning.

layers.label: 4 · Counterevidence and incentive
layers.text: The invoice result is one technically sophisticated person's anecdote, not a safety or success benchmark. Ghostty dominates some of his feed because it is his active project. The recommendation is scoped to method, not product adoption.

layers.label: 5 · Jerry activation
layers.text: For personal admin, begin with read-only search, a narrow output, an API-enforced communication boundary, and manual verification. Do not let the agent send, pay, dispute, or modify records on the first pass.

deepDives.title: Cheap code raises the ownership bar

source.paraphrase: If an agent wrote code you cannot understand, you cannot reliably debug or own it.

layers.label: 1 · Exact claim
layers.text: Generation makes code volume cheap; responsibility for debugging, reliability, and consequences remains with the person shipping it.

layers.label: 2 · Recent-feed pattern
layers.text: Four current posts repeat one coherent view: read code, ask basic questions, learn historical context, prototype alternatives, and split giant changes into semantic increments.

layers.label: 3 · Owned artifact
layers.text: Cindy's O'Reilly book and long-form observability writing establish real expertise in logs, traces, failure, debugging, and operational tradeoffs.

layers.label: 4 · Counterevidence and incentive
layers.text: These are expert judgments, not a randomized study of AI code review. Her lane is reliability, not model ranking. Low engagement is irrelevant to lane authority but means popularity did not select her.

layers.label: 5 · Jerry activation
layers.text: For one generated feature, draw the data and failure path, explain it without AI, split the diff, inject one safe failure, and repair it. If that is impossible, narrow the feature or require an expert review.

deepDives.title: Automate repeated judgment without automating away craft

source.paraphrase: Recurring review feedback should be encoded in tests, lint, CI, comments, skills, or project instructions.

layers.label: 1 · Exact claim
layers.text: The best engineers automate repeated work and repeated mistakes; agents multiply the value of domain knowledge already encoded in a repository.

layers.label: 2 · Recent-feed pattern
layers.text: This was the exceptional original in a current feed otherwise weighted toward Claude Code launches and colleague amplification. That supports Study, not automatic Core.

layers.label: 3 · Owned artifact
layers.text: Boris speaks from direct Claude Code product and engineering work. That makes him strong on the mechanism and team workflow, but affiliated on comparisons.

layers.label: 4 · Counterevidence and incentive
layers.text: A thoughtful reply warned that maniacal speed can destroy craft and produce more meaningless output. Anthropic benefits when teams encode work for Claude Code. The right synthesis is automation of known rejection classes plus preserved human product judgment.

layers.label: 5 · Jerry activation
layers.text: When Jerry gives the same correction twice, create one candidate guardrail. Prefer a deterministic validator or failing fixture; keep taste-heavy decisions as examples and human review rather than pretending every judgment is lintable.

deepDives.title: ‘Hard to evaluate’ can be a product smell

source.paraphrase: ‘Hard to evaluate’ can signal a product/interface problem rather than a missing grader.

layers.label: 1 · Exact claim
layers.text: An evaluation problem is sometimes downstream of an undefined user job: stakeholders cannot agree what ‘good’ means because the output surface is wrong.

layers.label: 2 · Recent-feed pattern
layers.text: Hamel repeatedly publishes trace review, failure taxonomy, human labeling, and judge-validation methods; he also posts course and community promotion.

layers.label: 3 · Owned artifact
layers.text: His evaluation guide exposes concrete production methods and their limitations rather than only advertising a score.

layers.label: 4 · Counterevidence and incentive
layers.text: He sells evaluation consulting, training, and a book, so complex eval programs align with his business. The product-smell framing is valuable partly because it argues against adding evaluation machinery too early.

layers.label: 5 · Jerry activation
layers.text: Before asking Codex to improve an output, name who decides, what observable change matters, and two examples of pass/fail. If that remains impossible, redesign or narrow the task before adding an AI judge.

deepDives.title: Autoresearch is a project, not a post Jerry can ‘use’

source.paraphrase: A coding agent repeatedly changes an experiment against a fixed evaluator and keeps improvements.

layers.label: 1 · Exact claim
layers.text: With a fast objective evaluator and a bounded codebase, an agent can iterate on research experiments and retain measured improvements.

layers.label: 2 · Recent-feed pattern
layers.text: Karpathy's current X profile is sparse and often repost-driven. His highest value lives in major owned artifacts and conceptual frames, not a guaranteed useful daily feed.

layers.label: 3 · Owned artifact
layers.text: The public autoresearch repository exposes the loop and code. That makes the experiment inspectable; it does not make it easy or universally transferable.

layers.label: 4 · Counterevidence and incentive
layers.text: The evaluator shapes and can be gamed by the optimizer; transfer to held-out tasks and larger systems must be tested. Network status also causes people he reposts to inherit attention they have not independently earned.

layers.label: 5 · Jerry activation
layers.text: The no-build lesson is enough for now: autonomy improves when feedback is objective and fast. Run autoresearch only after Jerry has a real experiment repo, metric he understands, reproducible sandbox, compute, version control, held-out checks, and at least a half-day to inspect failures.

methodology.selectionQuestion: Does this person repeatedly improve a decision Jerry can actually make, in a lane where their proof is real?

fiveLayers.name: Exact claim and conversation
fiveLayers.test: What did the post actually say, what does it not prove, and did replies or corrections change it?

fiveLayers.name: Recent-feed recurrence
fiveLayers.test: Across a current sample, is the value repeated or was this a lucky one-off? What is the noise?

fiveLayers.name: Owned or primary proof
fiveLayers.test: What did this person build, publish, measure, or maintain in the exact lane?

fiveLayers.name: Network, counterevidence, and incentive
fiveLayers.test: Who amplified it, where did the claim originate, what conflicts exist, and what serious objection survives?

fiveLayers.name: Jerry activation
fiveLayers.test: What changes now, what can be retained without building, and what prerequisites make implementation honest?

scoreRules: Lane credibility is scoped. Terraform does not create universal AI authority; Solidity security does not create general agent-privacy authority.
Popularity and verification are shown only as culture context. They add zero authority by themselves.
A respected repost is a discovery edge, never evidence about the reposted person's trustworthiness.
Core requires repeated current-feed value plus primary/owned proof and a Jerry-ready use. Study can be highly reputable but low cadence, advanced, or project-gated.
Radar is intentionally high-volume and lower-evidence. It is useful for outages, limits, memes, vocabulary, and network discovery—not final claims.
One event can move a scoped rating, but it cannot manufacture a whole-person record. Trust changes are dated rather than silently overwritten.

refresh.cadence: Run only as a substantial Codex review when the page is stale or a real decision requires it—not as a background timeline scraper.
refresh.owner: Jerry starts the review; Codex reads signed-in X read-only, owned artifacts, and recent personal task patterns, proposes changes, validates the bounded data, deploys, then records exact proof.
refresh.privacy: Store public-safe abstractions from personal tasks and representative public sources. Never store raw private threads, work/customer data, credentials, DMs, or full timelines.
refresh.noWrites: Refresh never follows, unfollows, likes, reposts, bookmarks, creates X Lists, posts, messages, or changes account settings.
